meta.title: Building Your First Chords
meta.summary: A chord is a scale with most of the notes taken out. Here is which ones stay.

spans.text: A chord is a scale with most of the notes taken out. Keep the
1st, 3rd and 5th
degrees, discard the other four, and what is left is a triad — three notes that describe a key so efficiently that one of them can go missing and your ear still fills it in.
Stacking thirds
Number the major scale
and sound degrees 1, 3 and 5 together. In C that is
C E G
. Both gaps are thirds: four frets from C up to E, then three from E up to G. Swap the size of those two gaps — three frets, then four — and the same three fingers give you a minor chord.
If you remember one thing from this article: the
third
decides the mood, and it is almost always the note your fretting hand moves by a single fret to change a chord from happy to sad.
Why a six-string chord has three notes
Strum an open
E minor
. Six strings ring, but only three note names are involved —
E
G
and
B
— several of them twice, in different octaves. That doubling is what makes a strummed guitar sound large. It is not extra harmony; it is the same three notes wearing a bigger coat.
It also explains why open E minor is the cheapest chord in music: two fingers, because four of the six strings are already sitting on the right note.

spans.text: C and D want the lowest strings kept quiet. A D chord with a low E booming underneath is not exactly wrong — it is a D/E — but it is blurred, and the blur is usually an accident.
Practise the change, not the chord
Anyone can hold a G if they are given ten seconds. The skill is arriving on it in time, and that is a separate thing to practise:

items.text: Set a timer for one minute and switch between
, one strum each. Count the clean changes.
Look for the finger that does not have to move. Between
your second finger barely travels — let it be the pivot.
Tomorrow, beat today's count by one. That is the entire method.
